title: Indo-Greeks
capsule: By the start of the dataset window (c. 126 BCE), the Indo-Greek realm founded by Demetrius I and brought to its height under Menander I had already fragmented into competing principalities across the Punjab, Gandhara, and the Paropamisadae. This late phase, centered increasingly on the eastern Punjab around Sagala (Sialkot), saw a brief revival under Apollodotus II (c. 80–65 BCE), who briefly recovered Taxila, followed by Hippostratus (c. 65–55 BCE), the last Greek king in the western Punjab before the Saka ruler Azes I expelled the Greeks from Taxila and Pushkalavati around 55 BCE. The line survived only in the east under Strato II and his son and co-regent Strato III, who issued bilingual Greek–Kharosthi coinage until the Indo-Scythian satrap Rajuvula of Mathura overran Sagala around 10 CE, ending the last Hellenistic kingdom in India.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The territory is reconstructed primarily from numismatic evidence and Ptolemaic geography; precise borders shifted continuously across more than 30 attested kings and are debated in modern scholarship.
